title: TB5-03096
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a permanent resident of Israel, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a permanent resident of Israel, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection. She has submitted new evidence in support of her appeal. The Appellant asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to set aside the determination of the RPD and either allow her claim for protection or refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed. Background

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that she is of Druze ethnicity and from the Golan Heights area of Israel. She is a permanent resident of Israel and holds a degree in XXXX. She experienced hostility and threats from her family and from the mainstream Druze community because of her sympathy for and work on behalf of Palestinian XXXX. She was sexually harassed by an employer, found herself monitored by Israeli intelligence while at another employer, and subsequently had difficulty finding suitable employment.

In June of 2011 the Appellant came to Canada to study, having secretly left home and escaped her controlling family. However, her scholarship was terminated early, and she made a refugee claim in October of 2014. Upon return to Israel, she fears harm at the hands of her family, Islamic extremists, and Israeli state agents.

The Appellant's application for refugee protection was heard on January 16, 2015. By a decision of February 24, 2015, the RPD rejected the claim. While it found the Appellant to be generally credible, it did not believe that there was a serious possibility she would be harmed by her family, and concluded that while she might face societal discrimination, this does not amount to persecution. The RPD also considered the issue of state protection, and found that the Appellant had not rebutted the presumption that Israel could provide her with adequate protection.

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD failed to provide adequate reasons for its findings, ignored evidence and submissions, erred in its assessment of persecution, and improperly applied the issue of state protection. The Appellant also asks the RAD to accept new evidence in support of her appeal. State Protection is Determinative

The RPD made a number of findings, including conclusions about credibility, discrimination vs. persecution, and state protection. The Appellant takes issues with almost all of those findings. In the RAD's view however, this appeal can be disposed of on the issue of state protection alone. That is, even if the RPD erred in its credibility analysis and in its consideration of the definition of persecution, this could not change the outcome of this appeal unless the state protection finding is also wrong.

The RAD had conducted an independent assessment of the availability of state protection for the Appellant in Israel. For reasons set out below, the RAD has reached the same conclusion as the RPD-that the Appellant has failed to rebut the presumption of adequate protection. It is therefore not necessary to consider the Appellant's arguments on the other issues contained in the RPD's reasons. ANALYSIS Admissibility of Evidence Submitted on Appeal

Section 110(4) of IRPA provides that an Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of her claim or that was not reasonably available, or that she could not reasonably have been expected2 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

It is for an Appellant to make full and detailed submissions in her Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of Section 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellant.3

While Section 110(4) provides the RAD with factors to consider in assessing a document's "newness," these factors alone cannot determine the admissibility of new evidence in an appeal. To put it simply, if a document is lacking in credibility, or is irrelevant, or is immaterial to the issues to be considered by the RAD, it would make little sense to admit such document, even if it meets the test in Section 110(4).

The RAD has, in many appeals to date, applied the factors set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in Raza.4 While Raza predates the introduction of IRPA Section 110(4), it is based on the nearly-identical wording of Section 113(a). The Court of Appeal held that new evidence should be considered for its credibility, relevance, newness, and materiality, in addition to any express statutory provisions.5

In Iyamuremye6, the Federal Court accepted the RAD's application of the factors in Raza to new evidence submitted on an appeal under IRPA. Subsequently, in Ghannadi,7 the Court held that the RAD should consider the factors in Raza, but noted that these are merely considerations to be taken into account and not necessarily determinative of admissibility. More recently the Court, in Singh,8 found that the factors in Raza are based specifically in the language of Section 113(a) and are not transferable in the context of an appeal before the RAD. The Court found that it was unreasonable for the RAD to strictly apply the Raza factors without distinguishing its own role from that of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) Officer who is bound by Section 113(a).9

In Singh, the Court wrote that ...in order for there to be a "full fact-based appeal" before the RAD, the criteria for the admissibility of evidence must be sufficiently flexible to ensure it can occur. Often, the evidence at stake will be essential for proving the factual basis of the errors the claimant alleges were made by the RPD. This consideration becomes all the more pertinent in light of the strict timelines a claimant now faces for initially submitting evidence before the RPD. A claimant now has 50 days to present all documents from the date he or she made the claim; the previous legislative scheme required the documents 20 days prior to a hearing, which, on average, took much longer to take place. When the RPD confronts a claimant on the weakness of his evidentiary record, the RAD should, in subsequent review of the decision, have some leeway in order to allow the claimant to respond to the deficiencies raised.10

The Court also held that the "main issue is whether the evidence 'was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably (or normally according to the French version) have been expected in the circumstances to have presented.'"11

The Court did not discuss Iyamuremye or Ghannadi in its analysis of Sections 110(4) and 113(a). It did, however, certify the following question: "In considering the role of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment officer and that of the Refugee Appeal Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board, sitting in appeal of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division, does the test set out in Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 for the interpretation of paragraph 113(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 apply to its subsection 110(4)?"12

While the certified question has not yet been answered, the RAD must nevertheless continue to consider new evidence, such as that which has been submitted in support of this appeal. While it may be inappropriate to strictly apply the factors in Raza, given that they are not specific to Section 110(4) and were not crafted for use in an appellate process, the RAD's consideration of new evidence cannot end with the application of the test in Section 110(4). To limit its analysis to that provision would be to ignore other provisions of IRPA-such as Sections 162(2) and 171(a.3)--as well as established jurisprudence based on statutory provisions almost identical to Section 110(4). Such a restricted analysis would also require the RAD to accept "new" evidence even if it is irrelevant, immaterial, or lacking in credibility.

The RAD presumes that Parliament, in creating Section 110(4), was well aware that this provision is almost identical in wording to Section 113(a)-which provides a strong indication that Parliament intended the test from Raza to be used by the RAD.13

In Denbel, the Federal Court held that "When interpreting legislative intent, the Court must give priority to the written text in the absence of any lexical ambiguity. The Court's opinions on best policy cannot supplant the text of the law; nor can select passages from the Hansard. In my view, Parliament intended these two provisions to enshrine the same legal test. If Parliament had intended to establish more flexible admissibility rules in RAD appeals, it would not have replicated the restrictive language which governs PRRAs."14

The RAD will therefore undertake an analysis of any proposed new evidence, not only for its timeliness, which is largely the focus of Section 110(4), but also for its evidentiary value. In doing so, the RAD will look to the factors in Raza but will not be strictly bound by them, and in applying any Raza factors must distinguish its own role from that of a PRRA officer.

Section 171(a.3) of IRPA allows the RAD to receive and base a decision on evidence that is adduced in the proceedings and considered "credible or trustworthy in the circumstances." This provision makes it clear that, in addition to the factors in Section 110(4), the RAD must consider the credibility and trustworthiness of proposed new evidence.

While IRPA makes specific reference to the credibility of evidence received by the RAD, there is no corresponding provision which addresses relevance. However, in the RAD's view, it is obvious that evidence must be assessed for its relevance.15 Apart from the support from the case law, it would be highly inefficient for the RAD to admit irrelevant evidence, and contrary to Section 162(2) of IRPA, which requires all divisions of the IRB to "deal with all proceedings before it as informally and quickly as the circumstances and the considerations of fairness and natural justice permit."
It is therefore appropriate for the RAD to consider whether new evidence is relevant, even if it meets the test in Section 110(4).

The RAD will also consider whether the proposed new evidence is material. In Raza, the Federal Court of Appeal described this factor: "Is the evidence material, in the sense that the refugee claim probably would have succeeded if the evidence had been made available to the RPD? If not, the evidence need not be considered." This factor may, in the RAD's view, set an inappropriately high standard in the context of a RAD appeal.

An officer determining a PRRA application must not engage in a review of the applicant's negative RPD decision. The PRRA process exists to determine whether a risk to the applicant has arisen between the date of issue of the RPD's decision and the date of the applicant's pending removal from Canada,16 and the officer has no power to reconsider or set aside the RPD's decision. A PRRA will in most cases take place a year or more after the RPD's decision.17 In this context, the definition of materiality set out in Raza makes good sense: the new evidence must be so significant that it would have led to a different outcome before the RPD.

However, as the Court noted in Singh, the RAD context is considerably different. The RAD is not restricted to making a new assessment of the risk faced by the Appellant, though this could occur as a result of new evidence presented upon appeal. The RAD appeal is meant to be decided within four or five months of the RPD's decision. The Appellant may challenge the decision of the RPD, and the RAD has broad powers to review that decision for errors of fact or law, or mixed fact and law, to confirm the decision, to confirm on other grounds, to set aside the decision and substitute another, or to set aside the determination and refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination. It is of paramount importance that the RAD may look only to admissible new evidence when considering whether to hold a hearing under Section 110(6).18

The Court's definition of materiality, which is appropriate for evidence presented in support of a PRRA application, seems overly restrictive when applied to evidence submitted in an appeal to the RAD. If the RAD would apply the materiality factor as set out in Raza, it could lead to the rejection of evidence that is capable of showing that the RPD's decision was in error, only because that evidence is not so strong that it would have resulted in the acceptance of the refugee claim had the evidence been before the RPD. Further, the RAD is not asking-as the PRRA officer is under Raza-whether the RPD decision would have been different. The RAD is considering whether the RAD thinks the determination should have been different or whether the RPD decision was in error.

For example, it is not uncommon for the RPD to reject a refugee claim on the basis that the claimant has not established his or her identity, and in such situations, the RPD is not required to go further to consider the evidence of persecution.19 A claimant rejected by the RPD on the basis of identity-perhaps because identity documents were still in transit from the country of origin at the time of the refugee hearing-might appeal to the RAD and present as new evidence such recently-received documents. However, those documents might be rejected by the RAD if it considers their materiality as defined in Raza: whether the refugee claim would probably have succeeded if the documents were made available to the RPD. In many cases, the establishment of identity does not in and of itself warrant the acceptance of a refugee claim, and therefore the Appellant's newly-obtained identity documents could be rejected by the RAD as lacking materiality.

In the RAD's view, this restrictive approach to materiality is not consistent with the broad powers given to the RAD. While the PRRA officer is required to focus on a single issue-risk to the applicant-the RAD is required to consider both whether the RPD decision is in error and, after having reviewed all of the evidence, whether the Appellant is a protected person. An approach that focuses on whether the evidence is material enough to affect the outcome of the RAD appeal rather than the RPD's decision is therefore preferred.

For these reasons, the RAD will apply the following factors to evidence that passes the test in Section 110(4). (a) The RAD will consider whether the proposed new evidence is credible and trustworthy. (b) The RAD will assess the relevance of the evidence-whether it is capable, together with the other evidence in the record (including other admissible new evidence) of proving or disproving a fact at issue in either the refugee claim or the appeal.20 (c) The RAD will determine whether the evidence is material, in the sense that it would be capable of justifying, with or without the benefit of an oral hearing, as the case may be, a disposition under section 111 of IRPA.

If the proposed new evidence does not meet each of the factors above, the RAD may choose not to admit it. These factors, however, are not exhaustive, as the RAD may consider other factors as appropriate in the circumstances.

The Appellant's proposed new evidence consists of the following documents: (a) A news article from an unclear source, dated February 14, 2014, entitled "Hundreds Commemorate the Anniversary of the Big Strike;"21 (b) A news article from "Tar Sands World," dated February 26, 2015, entitled "Israel drilling in Golan Heights violates international law;"22 (c) A report from "Tel Aviv Notes," dated March 10, 2015, entitled "Muslim and Druze in Israel: National, Patriotic, and Sectarian Loyalties in Conflict;"23 (d) An article from Ynet News, dated February 8, 2015, entitled "Druze soldier attacked after speaking Arabic;"24 (e) An article from Haaretz, dated March 5, 2015, entitled, "Mutual Mistrust Keeps Crime Flourishing in Israel's Arab Communities;"25 (f) An article from "Muslim News", dated March 4, 2015, entitled, "Syria: Israel detains 3 Syrians in Occupied Golan Heights;"26 (g) A weblog from "The Electronic Intifada," submitted on February 4, 2015, about the arrest by Israeli authorities of Palestinian politicians accused of participating in alleged terrorist organizations;27 (h) An opinion article from "AL Monitor," dated March 11, 2015, entitled, "Why is Israel Still Blind to Settler Violence Against Palestinians?"28 and (i) An article from ACRI (which the RAD presumes to be the Association for Civil Rights in Israel), dated March 12, 2015, entitled "'Blacklists' of East Jerusalem Residents Illegally Transferred from Police to Municipality."29

It is important to note here that the Appellant's refugee claim was rejected by a decision dated February 24, 2015, although it was not sent to the Appellant until a Notice of Decision was issued on March 10, 2015. For the purpose of Section 110(4), the rejection of the Appellant's claim took place on February 24, 2015.

The document in (a) did not arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim. The Appellant argues this article, which describes a pro-Syria demonstration in the Golan Heights, "confirms my evidence concerning the historical, social and political pressures on persons from the Golan Heights against taking Israeli citizenship."30 If this indeed is the purpose of the evidence, she could reasonably have been expected to present the document to the RPD through an application for post-hearing submission of documents. This document does not meet the test in Section 110(4). Even if the document did meet that test, however, the RAD would not admit it, as it is not relevant or material to the determinative issue of state protection.

The document in (b) reports that an "Egyptian expert" claims that Israel's drilling for oil in the Golan Heights violates international law. This article is dated two days after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim, and therefore meets the test in Section 110(4). However, this article is neither relevant nor material to the determinative issue of state protection, and therefore is not admissible in this appeal.

The document in (c) is dated March 10, 2015, after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim. The Appellant submits that this evidence "confirms my evidence concerning the complex nature of the Druze ethnic and religious identity, a minority within a minority in Israel."31 However, the RAD observes that, despite its recent date, the contents of this document are not new. They discuss issues that go back to 1948 and which culminated in violence within the Druze community in November of 2014. In Raza, the Federal Court of Appeal endorsed the principle that a document's "newness" cannot be tested solely by its date of creation; what is important is the event or circumstance sought to be proved by the evidence.32 The events and circumstances discussed in this document predate the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim. However, even if this document met the test in Section 110(4), it would not be admissible in this appeal, as it is not relevant and material to the issue of state protection.

The document in (d) is dated February 8, 2015, prior to the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim. The Appellant argues that this evidence "documents racially motivated attacks in Israel against Druze members of the IDF for merely speaking the Arabic language in public."33 What the Appellant does not provide is an explanation of why this document was not submitted to the RPD, which could be reasonably expected in the circumstances, given the nature of her claim. This document does not meet the test in Section 110(4). If the document did meet the test, the RAD would find it to be credible and relevant to the issue of state protection. However, it would not be found to be material, in the sense that it could justify a disposition of this appeal. The article speaks of two Druze soldiers who were attacked in public places for speaking Arabic. There is limited information about state protection; however, the article indicates that police had not interviewed one victim because he was unable to speak, and that the president of Israel telephoned the family of the second victim to offer condolences and support. Neither of these incidents assist the Appellant in rebutting the presumption of state protection, and therefore the document is not material.

The document in (e) is dated after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim and therefore could not have been submitted to the RPD. This document passes the test in Section 110(4). The RAD has no reason to doubt the credibility of the article, which speaks to the lack of trust between Israeli Arabs and the police. It is relevant to the issue of state protection as well. While the materiality of the document is dubious-it does not establish that the Israeli authorities are unwilling or unable to provide adequate protection to Arab Israelis, but rather that there are issues of mistrust between police and Arabs, though there have been some positive developments-the RAD will nevertheless admit it to assist in the analysis of state protection.

The document in (f) is dated after the rejection of the Appellant's claim. It is a news article which, in the Appellant's submission, confirms "my evidence concerning the aggressive actions of the Israeli security forces against perceived political opponents in the occupied Golan Heights."34 With respect to the Appellant, this is a rather questionable description of the article. The article, which notes that Israel and Syria are still officially at war, reports that Israel detained a man described by Syria as a "Syrian freedom fighter" as well as two other Syrians in the Golan Heights.35 As the RAD reads this evidence, it does not establish aggressive actions against "perceived political opponents," but rather the detention of a "freedom fighter" from a country with which Israel is in a state of war, as well as two other men from that country. This evidence is not relevant or material to this appeal or to the determinative issue of state protection.

The document in (g) is a weblog which discusses the Israeli detention of Palestinian lawmakers. The document appears to have been published on April 2, 2015, and thus post-dates the rejection of the Appellant's claim; she argues that this document "further confirms my evidence concerning the aggressive actions of the Israeli security forces against perceived political opponents."36 Even if this document meets the test in Section 110(4), it is not admissible, as it is not credible or trustworthy. It appears to be a weblog by an author about whom no information is provided; it is not at all clear where the information in the article comes from, or whether it is true. While there is a reference to "United Press International" at the top of the article, this appears to be as part of a photo credit. This document is from an unknown source and its reliability cannot be determined; it is not admissible here.

The document in (h) is an opinion piece about violence by Israeli settlers toward Palestinians. It is dated March 11, 2015, after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim. The Appellant argues that this "provides a more detailed picture of these attacks and from which I believe no impartial observer can conclude that the State of Israel provides adequate protection for the victims or those at risk of such attacks."37 In the RAD's view, this document suffers from the same deficiencies as document (i). Its "author" is Akiva Elder, and there is no indication of who this person is or how the information was obtained. The website URL indicate that this was posted in a section called "originals," which does not suggest that it was a news report. The tone of the document itself makes clear that it is an opinion piece: "The experience of recent years shows that the vision of coexistence between settlers and their Palestinian neighbours, a coexistence between a horse and its rider, is nothing but an illusion. The horse kicks, the rider whips it with his crop and eventually both collapse."38 The RAD finds that this document is not a news article or a report from an independent organization; it appears to be the opinion of an individual. The RAD has no way of knowing who that individual is, or whether the facts and statistics reported in the document are accurate. The RAD finds that this document is not credible or trustworthy, and declines to admit it in this appeal.

Finally, the document in (i) is a report from what appears to be the Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI). The document is dated March 12, 2015 and therefore postdates the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim. The report explains that ACRI has sent an urgent letter to Israel's attorney general asking him to investigate a journalist's exposé, which claimed that police provided East Jerusalem municipal officials with "blacklists" of residents suspected of participating in disturbances and riots. According to the report, ACRI is concerned that the sharing of these lists will result in municipal enforcement measures which could be as severe as house demolitions. ACRI asks the attorney general to begin an investigation.

The RAD has no reason to doubt the credibility of this document, and it is relevant to the matter of state protection. However, it is not, in the RAD's view, material in the sense that it could justify a disposition here. ACRI has raised concerns about information contained in a journalist's report, and has asked the authorities to open an investigation. There is no information about whether the alleged practice was investigated, or found to have occurred, or how the authorities have responded to any violations found. As such, this document contains unproven allegations with no information about how the state responded, and therefore does little to rebut the presumption of state protection. This document is not admitted in this appeal.
For these reasons, the RAD accepts the document in (e), but declines to admit the Appellant's other proposed new evidence. Request for an Oral Hearing
The Appellant asks that the RAD order an oral hearing pursuant to Section 110(6), if it deems this appropriate.

Section 110(3) of IRPA requires that the RAD proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD record, while allowing the RAD to accept documentary evidence and submissions from the Minister and the Appellant. The person who is the subject of the appeal may, pursuant to Section 110(4), present "only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection."

According to Section 110(6) the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, that is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. In this appeal, where there is no evidence from or in response to the Minister, the documentary evidence referred to in Section 110(3) must be understood in relation to Section 110(4).

When read together, Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new (Section 110(4)) evidence, in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

While the RAD has admitted one piece of the Appellant's proposed new evidence, that document does not raise a serious issue with respect to her credibility, nor can it justify allowing or rejecting her refugee claim. The RAD therefore finds it would not be appropriate to order an oral hearing in this appeal. What is the Role of the RAD?
While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.

The Appellant submits that the RAD owes no deference to the RPD in this case, that the RAD should review the RPD's interpretation and application of the law on a standard of correctness, and that the RAD should conduct its own independent assessment of the evidence and issues raised by the Appellant in her refugee claim.

In another decision, this panel considered at some length the legislation and jurisprudence concerning the role of the RAD.39 It assessed the nature of a RAD appeal and addressed the scope and degree of deference to be shown to findings of the RPD. The panel reached the following conclusions, which it finds to also be applicable here, about the approach to be taken in a RAD appeal. The RAD's Approach

The RAD will take the following approach in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD. It will assess all of the evidence, both that in the RPD's record and any admissible new evidence. It will consider questions of law, fact, and mixed law and fact raised by the Appellant and, where applicable, the Respondent.

Where the proceeding is a true appeal-that is, where there is no admissible new evidence-the RAD will consider the decision of the RPD, the submissions in respect of that decision, and determine whether the RPD's determination is wrong. As a true appeal is founded on the record, the RAD must conduct an independent assessment of the evidence in that record in order to determine the appeal.

Where an appeal includes admissible new evidence that speaks to an error in the RPD's decision, it is a hybrid appeal, where the RAD must consider the RPD's reasons in light of the new evidence, which may establish that the decision of the RPD is wrong.40

Where an appeal presents admissible new evidence which establishes a new, changed, or heightened risk, or otherwise changes the overall nature of the claim, this will result in a limited de novo appeal. In some such cases, the decision of the RPD may be less relevant in light of the new evidence-that is, the new evidence establishes a risk or degree of risk, or other potentially determinative matter not considered by the RPD. Unlike a true de novo proceeding, however, the RAD will not ignore the RPD's record or the findings of the lower tribunal, as these may remain relevant to the appeal.

The RAD will recognize and respect findings which the RPD was in an advantageous position to make, which will normally include credibility findings and other findings of fact. Where such deference is to be shown, the RAD will not intervene unless the RPD's reasoning process is not comprehensible or the outcome of that process is not based on and supported by the evidence.

Where the RPD's determination is entirely based on findings which warrant deference-such as an overall lack of credibility, based on oral testimony-the RAD will, having conducted its own assessment of the evidence, consider whether the RPD's reasoning process is comprehensible and whether the determination is based on and supported by the evidence.

On matters where the RPD has no advantage, the RAD will show no deference and will apply a standard of correctness, engaging in its own analysis of the evidence and reaching its own conclusion to determine if the RPD was wrong. Where the RAD finds that its conclusion does not agree with that of the RPD, the RAD will substitute its own finding and determination or, if it is unable to substitute, will refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination. State Protection

The RPD noted well-established law that a state is presumed capable of protecting its citizens, and that it is for a refugee claimant to provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The panel correctly noted that while the test for such protection is one of adequacy, state protection must be effective to be considered adequate.

The RPD considered the Appellant's testimony that she never approached the state for protection of any sort. It noted that, after suffering sexual harassment, she did not approach the police because her parents told her not to, as the perpetrator was a former police officer and they presumed the police would not act against him. The RAD correctly observed that a subjective reluctance to engage the state cannot be used to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection. In the RAD's view, one's reluctance to approach the authorities cannot in itself be used as proof that the authorities would not provide protection.

The RAD Rules require the Appellant to include in her Memorandum full and detailed submissions about errors allegedly made by the RPD, including the location of those errors in the decision or transcript. While the Appellants' Memorandum does not challenge the RPD's analysis of evidence relating to state protection, it raises a brief but significant challenge to the panel's very consideration of the issue. The Appellant argues that, while the RPD acknowledged that she is stateless, it erred in requiring her to nevertheless rebut the presumption of state protection. She points out that Section 96(b) of IRPA, which deals with stateless individuals, makes no reference to state protection, and submits that it therefore was a fundamental error of law for the RPD to engage in a state protection analysis. She cites the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Thabet, which notes that in the case of stateless claimants, the question of protection does not arise, as persons who are stateless "are without recourse to state protection."41

It is helpful here to review the purpose of the state protection provisions in IRPA. In Ward, the Supreme Court endorsed the presumption of state protection, and explained, "Although this presumption increases the burden on the claimant, it does not render illusory Canada's provision of a haven for refugees. The presumption serves to reinforce the underlying rationale of international protection as a surrogate, coming into play where no alternative remains to the claimant. Refugee claims were never meant to allow a claimant to seek out better protection than that from which he or she benefits already."42

The UNHCR Handbook explains, "Whenever the protection of the country of nationality is available, and there is no ground based on well-founded fear for refusing it, the person concerned is not in need of international protection and is not a refugee."43

It seems clear, both from Canadian jurisprudence and the UNHCR's guidance, that Canada's protection is a surrogate which is to be offered where there is no alternative protection available to the refugee claimant.

Prior to June of 2002, refugee protection in Canada was determined on the basis of the Immigration Act.44 Claims for protection were assessed on the basis of Convention grounds. When the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act came into force in June of 2002, it provided "complementary protection;" that is, it offered Canada's protection not only to Convention refugees, but also to "persons in need of protection," as set out in Section 97.

While Section 96-which is based on the refugee Convention-does not consider the issue of state protection for stateless claimants, Section 97 is different. Referring both to nationals and to those who do not have a country of nationality, Section 97 offers protection to those who face a risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment and "is unable or, because of that risk, unwilling to avail themselves of the protection of that country."

It seems, then, that where the refugee claim of a stateless individual has nexus to a Convention ground, he or she is not required to rebut the presumption of state protection, while a person who faces a risk that is not related to a Convention ground must establish that protection is not available in the country of last habitual residence.

Was it an error for the RPD to consider the issue of state protection in the Appellant's refugee claim? The claim was made under Section 96, as the Appellant fears persecution because of Convention grounds including ethnicity and political opinion, as well as the gender-based particular social group.

In the RAD's view, the Appellant's status in Israel is important. It seems apparent that the UNHCR Handbook considers "stateless" as those persons with no country to which they can return: "In the case of a stateless refugee, the question of 'availment of protection' of the country of his former habitual residence does not, of course, arise. Moreover, once a stateless person has abandoned the country of his former habitual residence for the reasons indicated in the definition, he is usually unable to return."45

While the Appellant here may technically be stateless, in the sense that she does not hold citizenship of Israel or any other country, she does not fit the description in the Handbook, or even in Thabet, which describes stateless persons as those without recourse to state protection. To put it simply, she does have access to state protection. The evidence before the RPD and the RAD does not establish that Israel refuses to provide protection to permanent residents. When the Appellant was sexually harassed and did not report this to the police, it was not because of her lack of citizenship, but because of her parents' belief that such reporting would be futile.

In the RAD's view, the Appellant is not entitled to Canada's surrogate protection if alternative protection is available to her. The application of state protection to her claim does not arise out of the language of Section 96(b), but rather out of Section 96 itself. That provision requires that a Convention refugee have a "well-founded fear of persecution."

This matter is somewhat similar to that heard by the Federal Court in Vetcels.46 There the applicants were non-citizen residents of Latvia, and the RPD rejected their claims on the basis of state protection. They argued to the Federal Court, as the Appellant submits to the RAD, that Section 96(b) does not include the principle of state protection. The Court upheld the RPD's finding and dismissed the application for judicial review.

The Court relied upon an earlier decision, Popov, which also discussed the position of a stateless person with respect to state protection.47 That judgement, which also considered Thabet, made a link between state protection and the well-foundedness of a fear of persecution: "...they must prove not only a subjective fear but also an objective fear. This requires that they rebut the presumption of state protection and are "required to prove that they exhausted all the domestic avenues available to them before without success before claiming refugee status in Canada" (Hinzman at paragraph 46)."48

The evidence does not establish that Israel is unable or unwilling to provide adequate protection to permanent residents such as the Appellant. To establish that her fear of persecution is well-founded, the Appellant must prove an objective basis for that fear. To prove that her fear has such objective basis, she must rebut the presumption of state protection.
For these reasons, it was not an error for the RPD to consider the issue of state protection in the determination of the Appellant's refugee claim.

The Appellant's Memorandum does not challenge the RPD's state protection analysis itself or identify errors therein. The Federal Court has described the statutory configuration of an appeal to the RAD: "In sum, the appeal before the RAD (i) is directed at the decision of the RPD, (ii) unless new evidence is accepted, is to be entertained on the basis of the record as it was constituted at the time of the RPD's decision, and (iii) is to be concerned solely with the errors of law, of fact or of mixed fact and law that, according to the appellant, the RPD made."49 While the Rules require the Appellant to make full and detailed submissions in her Memorandum about any alleged errors and their location, she has not done so here.

However, the RAD has accepted a piece of new evidence which has some relevance to the issue of state protection. Document (e) is an article about the relationship between Arab Israelis and the police. The document reports that "The 'rule of law' seems absent in many Arab enclaves in Israel, where deadly weapons abound, local protection rackets tyrannize residents, and feuds too easily turn fatal."50 It explains that Arab-Israelis, many of whom have never had contact with the police, believe that law enforcement is afraid to help them or does not care to. Police report that local residents hinder, rather than help, their investigations. The article gives examples of both ineffective and effective policing for Israeli Arabs. The document concludes, "A shift in perception is in order. Palestinian citizens must come to believe that the police are there to help them, and police must see Palestinian citizens as their clients, rather than their adversaries."

While this article is helpful in providing context to the issue of state protection for Arab Israelis, it is simply not a clear and convincing rebuttal of the presumption of state protection, particularly with respect to Druze residents of Israel. It indicates that Arab-Israelis distrust the police and are reluctant to cooperate with them, and that the police do not always act effectively, but this does not establish that the police will not provide protection to someone such as the Appellant.

Israel is a democratic country, and there is a presumption that it can provide adequate state protection. The onus is on the Appellant to rebut that presumption with clear and convincing evidence; the onus is not on the RPD, or the RAD, to establish that adequate state protection exists.51 The RPD considered the evidence with respect to state protection, and the RAD has considered further evidence. Although the Appellant objected to the very consideration of state protection, she has not explained in her Memorandum, as required, where the RPD erred in its consideration of the evidence.

[Given that the Appellant raised no allegations as to errors in the RPD's analysis of state protection and h]aving considered the evidence, the RAD reaches the same conclusion as did the RPD:52 the Appellant has not rebutted the presumption of adequate state protection in Israel, and is therefore not entitled to Canada's surrogate protection.53 Application of the Gender Guidelines

The Appellant argues that the RPD did not apply the Chairperson's Guidelines on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution ("the Gender Guidelines") and that its mere mention of the Guidelines in its reasons is not sufficient.

In her affidavit the Appellant declares that she was "unable to discern how the RPD member applied the principles and framework of analysis set out in the guidelines in my case. In particular I cannot see that the RPD member understood and considered the importance of the social, cultural and religious contexts of my claim of which the Guidelines suggest the decision maker should be cognizant when addressing, for instance, the question of why a woman might not seek state protection."54 The Appellant later argues that the RPD "misinterprets and disparages" a psychotherapist's letter, which, in the Appellant's opinion, "is a good example of her insensitive attitude toward my case and her failure to apply the principles set out in the Guidelines...."55

The Gender Guidelines exist to ensure that gender-based claims are heard with sensitivity.56 The Appellant, despite her allegations, has not demonstrated how the RPD failed to hear her claim with sensitivity. The RPD considered the Appellant's status as a woman,57 her experience with gender inequality,58 her allegation of sexual harassment,59 and assessed the risk she faced as a "single, educated woman from a traditional Druze family."60 The panel also considered her "stated difficulties because of her gender and ethnicity...."61 When it considered state protection for the Appellant, it did so in the context of her profile as "an Arab woman." It considered her failure to approach the authorities about an incident of sexual harassment, noting her testimony that she considered a civil suit but could not afford it, and that her parents discouraged her from making a criminal complaint because the perpetrator was a former police officer.62

The Appellant wrote in her Basis of Claim narrative that, in dealing with the harassment, "I felt helpless as a woman without power in a male dominated society."63 The RPD did not dispute this evidence, nor does the RAD doubt that the Appellant felt this way. However, this feeling does not rebut the presumption of state protection, or do anything to prove that the Israeli police would not have assisted the Appellant had she complained.

The RPD considered the psychotherapist's letter64 and noted that it does not indicate details of the claimant's experiences or her treatment, and found the letter to be of little evidentiary value. The Appellant argues that the RPD's dismissal of this letter showed insensitivity to the Gender Guidelines. The RAD disagrees. The letter makes vague but bold claims, such as "She suffered hard in this masculine and traditional community and every minute was a nightmare for her" and "She has been struggling very hard to express herself through her academic and human achievement." The therapist writes, "I worked with XXXX for a long time, helping her dealing with the threat and danger she used to face." It is difficult to see how the RPD could have given this letter much weight.

There is nothing in the recording of the proceedings or in the RPD's decision itself that indicates a lack of sensitivity to gender issues or a disregard of the Gender Guidelines. The Gender Guidelines do not shield the Appellant's testimony from the RPD's scrutiny or give weight to documents that otherwise do not have probative value.

There are two observations that should be made here. One is that, though the Rules require the Appellant to make full and detailed submissions in her Memorandum, she in essence provided two detailed memoranda: her own lengthy affidavit, as well as counsel's Memorandum. In the RAD's view, there was no requirement to consider arguments made in the affidavit, as they should have been in the Memorandum. The RAD did consider the Affidavit insofar as it provided information about proposed new evidence. However, this information should have been included, pursuant to the Rules, in the Memorandum.

Second, the Appellant repeatedly argues that the RPD did not refer to particular pieces of evidence, or portions of testimony, or submissions of her counsel before the RPD. As the issue of state protection is determinative here, the RAD has not reviewed all of the Appellant's many challenges to other findings of the lower tribunal. However, as the Appellant may find that the RAD also did not address each fact or document or submission to the extent she would have preferred, the RAD observes that the tribunal is presumed to have considered all of the evidence before it, and there is no requirement for the panel to refer to each document in the record.65 It is not an error for the RPD to summarize the allegations and arguments in a refugee claim, as long as it is clear that the panel understood the facts and the submissions. Here the RAD has not addressed each of the Appellant's many challenges and arguments because this panel has found the issue of state protection to be determinative.

The Appellant has not rebutted the presumption of adequate state protection in Israel, and therefore is not entitled to Canada's surrogate protection. Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed.
